internship.title: Web Application Security Internship
internship.description: A research-backed internship program focused specifically on assessing and improving the security of web applications. It combines structured security testing, secure engineering, controlled manual assessment, code review, automated regression testing and professional reporting. Practical work is limited to applications and environments the intern owns or is explicitly authorized to test.
internship.level: Intermediate progressing to advanced practical assessment

duration.basis: The program contains 8 progressive modules, module-level engineering tasks, a hands-on capstone and a final assessment. The exact calendar depends on prior HTTP, Python and Git experience.

prerequisites: Basic Python or another scripting language.
Comfort reading web requests and responses.
objectives: Perform authorized web application security testing using a repeatable methodology.
Understand authentication, authorization, sessions and browser trust boundaries.
Identify and remediate injection, XSS, CSRF, SSRF, file-upload and configuration risks in controlled environments.
Use secure code review and automated regression tests to verify remediation.
Produce evidence-based security findings and retest results.

competencies.name: Assessment planning
competencies.evidence: Scope document, asset inventory and WSTG-aligned coverage matrix.

competencies.name: HTTP analysis
competencies.evidence: Captured request/response evidence and endpoint inventory.

competencies.name: Authentication and session testing
competencies.evidence: Cookie review, login tests and session lifecycle reasoning.

competencies.name: Authorization testing
competencies.evidence: Cross-user object-level and role-level regression tests.

competencies.name: Secure coding
competencies.evidence: Parameterized SQL, validation, safe templating and secret handling.

competencies.name: Security testing
competencies.evidence: pytest regression suite plus controlled manual tests.

competencies.name: Reporting
competencies.evidence: Reproducible findings with impact, remediation and retest fields.

competencies.name: Engineering judgment
competencies.evidence: Architecture decisions, limitations and explicit assumptions.

technologyStack.name: Python
technologyStack.selectionReason: Useful for focused HTTP test harnesses and the capstone implementation.

technologyStack.name: Flask 3.1.3
technologyStack.selectionReason: Current documented Flask 3.1 release during research and simple enough to expose security boundaries.

technologyStack.name: SQLite
technologyStack.selectionReason: Self-contained relational storage for deterministic lab work.

technologyStack.name: Browser developer tools and an intercepting proxy
technologyStack.selectionReason: Directly exposes browser and server behavior needed for web assessment.

technologyStack.name: OWASP WSTG
technologyStack.selectionReason: Provides structured web application security testing guidance.

modules.title: Security Assessment Foundations and Scope
modules.description: Build the professional foundation for authorized web application security testing: scope, rules of engagement, asset inventory, evidence handling, HTTP fundamentals and repeatable test planning.
objectives: Define an authorized assessment boundary and distinguish in-scope from out-of-scope behavior.
Read HTTP requests and responses well enough to identify trust boundaries and security-relevant data.
Create a repeatable test plan and evidence trail instead of ad-hoc probing.
Use Git and disciplined notes for reproducible security work.

lessons.title: Authorization, Scope and Rules of Engagement
lessons.description: Security testing is useful only when the tester knows exactly what is authorized. The intern learns scope statements, safe handling of credentials, evidence discipline, stopping conditions and the difference between a lab, a staging environment and an Internet target.
learningObjectives: Create a safe test plan with objectives, exclusions and stopping conditions.
Recognize when a requested test needs explicit approval.
lessons.notes: A professional assessment begins with authorization, asset identification, objectives, assumptions, communication paths and evidence rules. NIST SP 800-115 describes planning and conducting technical security tests and analyzing findings. Use it as a methodology reference, not as permission to test arbitrary targets.

practicals.question: Which item belongs in a rules-of-engagement document?
options: An in-scope hostname and testing window
A claim that testing is always safe
practicals.answer: An in-scope hostname and testing window
practicals.explanation: Scope and timing turn a technical action into an authorized assessment activity.

quiz.question: Which item belongs in a rules-of-engagement document?
options: An in-scope hostname and testing window
A claim that testing is always safe
quiz.answer: An in-scope hostname and testing window
quiz.explanation: Scope and timing turn a technical action into an authorized assessment activity.

lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from Authorization, Scope and Rules of Engagement during authorized assessment and remediation work.

lessons.title: HTTP Request and Response Anatomy
lessons.description: HTTP is the primary evidence stream for web security testing. Learn methods, URLs, parameters, headers, cookies, bodies, status codes, redirects and content types.
learningObjectives: Trace a user action through its HTTP representation.
Distinguish path, query, header, cookie and body inputs.
lessons.notes: Treat client-controlled values as untrusted. The browser is not a security boundary. A tester should inspect the server response directly instead of inferring security only from the user interface.

practicals.title: Capture and classify one complete request/response exchange
instructions: Use an intentionally controlled local web application or a training lab you are authorized to test.
Capture one GET and one state-changing request in browser developer tools or an intercepting proxy.
Record method, path, query parameters, headers, cookies, content type, response status and relevant response headers.
Mark which fields are user-controlled and which security controls appear to protect them.
Write three test hypotheses without changing server state beyond the lab workflow.
practicals.deliverable: A short request inventory containing two exchanges, trust-boundary notes and three test hypotheses.

lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from HTTP Request and Response Anatomy during authorized assessment and remediation work.

lessons.title: Threat Modeling and Trust Boundaries
lessons.description: Turn an application description into security questions by identifying assets, actors, trust boundaries, entry points and high-value actions.
learningObjectives: Identify high-risk entry points and sensitive operations.
lessons.notes: Threat modeling is a design and testing aid. A useful model connects a business action to an asset, an actor and a control that should enforce the intended behavior.
lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from Threat Modeling and Trust Boundaries during authorized assessment and remediation work.

lessons.title: Evidence, Findings and Git-Based Workflow
lessons.description: A security finding is more useful when another engineer can reproduce it. Learn issue statements, evidence quality, severity reasoning, remediation notes and a simple branch/commit workflow.
learningObjectives: Write a concise finding with evidence and impact.
Use small commits and meaningful messages for security work.
lessons.notes: Keep secrets out of repositories. Record timestamps, target, endpoint, test condition and evidence while avoiding unnecessary sensitive data.
lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from Evidence, Findings and Git-Based Workflow during authorized assessment and remediation work.

lessons.title: Testing Methodology with OWASP WSTG and NIST SP 800-115
lessons.description: Use established methodology instead of inventing a checklist. Map reconnaissance, configuration review, identity tests, input tests, business-logic checks and reporting to a repeatable process.
learningObjectives: Use the OWASP WSTG structure to organize a web assessment.
Relate test planning to NIST SP 800-115 concepts.
lessons.notes: OWASP WSTG is a comprehensive web security testing resource and includes methodology, application testing, reporting and tools guidance.

quiz.question: What is the main reason to use a testing guide such as WSTG?
options: To make testing repeatable and coverage-oriented
quiz.answer: To make testing repeatable and coverage-oriented
quiz.explanation: A testing guide improves consistency and coverage but does not guarantee findings or replace tester judgment.

lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from Testing Methodology with OWASP WSTG and NIST SP 800-115 during authorized assessment and remediation work.

tasks.title: Create an authorized assessment plan for a local target
tasks.description: Create a one-page assessment plan for a fictional internal application running on localhost.
tasks.problemStatement: The engineering team needs a repeatable plan that defines scope, assets, objectives, constraints, evidence handling and stopping conditions before testing begins.
objectives: Define in-scope assets and exclusions.
Create test categories and evidence requirements.
Describe safe stopping and escalation conditions.
requirements: Use localhost or a documented training VM only.
Include authentication assumptions and test accounts as placeholders rather than real credentials.
Include a coverage checklist mapped to WSTG areas.
constraints: Do not scan or test public assets.
Do not include credentials or secrets in the plan.
tasks.hint: Start with assets, objectives and rules of engagement before tool commands.
tasks.solutionCode:
ASSESSMENT PLAN
Scope: http://127.0.0.1:5000 only.
Assets: local training application, local SQLite database.
Objectives: authentication, session, authorization, injection, XSS, CSRF, headers, error handling.
Excluded: denial-of-service, destructive actions, credential attacks against real accounts, third-party systems.
Evidence: request/response pair, screenshot when useful, endpoint, timestamp, reproduction steps.
Stopping: stop on unexpected data exposure, service instability or any out-of-scope dependency.
Reporting: every finding includes evidence, impact, remediation and regression test recommendation.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The solution is a compact scope document that makes later testing reproducible and bounded.

modules.assessment: The intern is evaluated on scope discipline, clarity and evidence quality.

modules.title: Reconnaissance, Attack Surface Mapping and HTTP Testing
modules.description: Map the reachable web attack surface, identify endpoints and input locations, and learn controlled manual and automated HTTP testing without treating a tool result as proof.
objectives: Build an endpoint inventory from browser and HTTP evidence.
Identify parameters, cookies, forms, APIs and alternative routes.
Use controlled request automation with timeouts and explicit targets.
Differentiate enumeration from exploitation and preserve evidence.

lessons.title: Attack Surface Inventory
lessons.description: Inventory routes, forms, APIs, static assets, authentication entry points and administrative functions.
learningObjectives: Identify state-changing routes and sensitive functions.
lessons.notes: A route is not only a URL. Method, content type, authentication state and parameters change the security properties of an endpoint.
lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from Attack Surface Inventory during authorized assessment and remediation work.

lessons.title: Proxy-Based Request Inspection
lessons.description: Use an intercepting proxy to understand how browsers construct requests and how server responses reveal security controls.
learningObjectives: Capture and replay requests within scope.
lessons.notes: Burp Suite and OWASP ZAP are useful for controlled inspection. The intern should understand each request before replaying or modifying it.
lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from Proxy-Based Request Inspection during authorized assessment and remediation work.

lessons.title: Safe HTTP Automation with Requests
lessons.description: Use Python Requests for small, deterministic test harnesses that target only an explicit URL and fail safely.
learningObjectives: Avoid uncontrolled crawling or high-rate activity.
lessons.notes: Requests supports common HTTP methods, sessions, cookies and timeouts. Use it for focused verification rather than indiscriminate scanning.

quiz.question: Why should a security test harness set a timeout?
options: To prevent a hanging request from blocking the test run
quiz.answer: To prevent a hanging request from blocking the test run
quiz.explanation: Explicit timeouts make automation predictable and help prevent accidental resource consumption.

lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from Safe HTTP Automation with Requests during authorized assessment and remediation work.

tasks.title: Build a focused endpoint inventory script
tasks.description: Create a small Python script that requests a provided list of local URLs and records response status, content type and selected security headers.
tasks.problemStatement: A tester needs a repeatable baseline inventory without introducing broad crawling or high request volume.
objectives: Read targets from an explicit local file.
Apply a fixed timeout.
Record status, content type, HSTS, CSP, X-Content-Type-Options and Referrer-Policy.
Handle connection errors cleanly.
requirements: Use Python and Requests.
Only accept http://127.0.0.1/ or http://localhost/ targets.
Use GET only.
tasks.hint: Build the URL allow-list before creating the HTTP session.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The script restricts the target to loopback, uses GET only, fixes request timeouts and records a small set of security-relevant response properties. This is suitable for controlled local assessment work.
tasks.validation: Run against a targets.txt file containing only localhost URLs and compare the output with browser/proxy observations.

modules.assessment: The intern must demonstrate target discipline and accurate interpretation of HTTP evidence.

modules.title: Identity, Authentication and Session Security
modules.description: Assess login flows, credential handling, session lifecycle and cookie protections, and understand how authentication failures differ from authorization failures.
objectives: Differentiate authentication, session management and authorization.
Assess login workflows, password storage controls and session lifecycle.
Inspect cookie attributes including Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite.
Recognize session fixation and weak session handling risks.

lessons.title: Authentication versus Authorization
lessons.description: Authentication establishes identity; authorization determines what an authenticated identity may do.
learningObjectives: Identify missing or misplaced access checks.
Test both positive and negative authorization cases.
lessons.notes: OWASP Authentication guidance recommends strong transport for login and authenticated pages and reauthentication for sensitive changes. Authorization must still be enforced server-side.
lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from Authentication versus Authorization during authorized assessment and remediation work.

lessons.title: Password Storage and Login Defenses
lessons.description: Learn why passwords must not be stored in plaintext, how modern password hashing differs from encryption, and how authentication endpoints should resist common abuse.
learningObjectives: Identify hard-coded credentials and unsafe password storage.
lessons.notes: A web application should not expose credentials or sensitive internal accounts through public UI. Use framework-supported password hashing and secret management.
lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from Password Storage and Login Defenses during authorized assessment and remediation work.

lessons.title: Session Lifecycle and Cookie Security
lessons.description: Assess session creation, rotation, expiry, invalidation and cookie attributes.
learningObjectives: Check HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite properties.
Explain why session identifiers are high-value secrets.
lessons.notes: OWASP's Session Management guidance treats session identifiers as highly sensitive and recommends secure lifecycle handling. MDN documents Set-Cookie behavior and attribute semantics.

quiz.question: What does HttpOnly primarily protect?
options: It prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie value
quiz.answer: It prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie value
quiz.explanation: HttpOnly reduces cookie disclosure through scripts, but it does not stop the browser from sending the cookie with requests.

lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from Session Lifecycle and Cookie Security during authorized assessment and remediation work.

lessons.title: Sensitive Actions and Reauthentication
lessons.description: Learn when applications should require fresh authentication for password changes and other high-risk actions.
lessons.notes: Reauthentication reduces the impact of stolen sessions and attacks that reach sensitive functions.
lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from Sensitive Actions and Reauthentication during authorized assessment and remediation work.

tasks.title: Review session cookie configuration
tasks.description: Given a captured Set-Cookie header from a local training application, assess the security attributes and write a corrected configuration.
tasks.problemStatement: The application currently sets a session cookie but the development team is unsure whether the attributes provide appropriate protection for a production HTTPS deployment.
objectives: Inspect Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite.
Explain local development versus production configuration.
Recommend a safe cookie name and scope.
requirements: Use a local application only.
Do not include live credentials.
Reference MDN and OWASP session guidance.
constraints: Do not claim that one cookie configuration fits every architecture.
Do not recommend storing tokens in localStorage for convenience.
tasks.hint: Check whether the cookie is carrying authenticated session state and whether the deployment uses HTTPS.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The review logic deliberately distinguishes properties that can be checked mechanically from architectural decisions that need context. MDN documents cookie semantics; OWASP adds security rationale.

modules.assessment: The intern must accurately distinguish AuthN, AuthZ and session controls.

modules.title: Authorization, Access Control and Business Logic
modules.description: Test whether server-side controls actually enforce object ownership, role restrictions and business rules, with emphasis on horizontal and vertical authorization.
objectives: Test object ownership and role boundaries.
Recognize IDOR/BOLA and function-level authorization failures.
Reason about business logic beyond input validation.
Write authorization findings with reproducible evidence.

lessons.title: Object-Level Authorization
lessons.description: Learn to test whether one identity can access another user's resources by changing identifiers or routes in authorized lab scenarios.
learningObjectives: Distinguish predictable identifiers from authorization decisions.
lessons.notes: Authorization must be enforced on the server for the requested object and action; hiding links in the UI is not an access control boundary.

quiz.question: What should prevent a user from reading another user's record even if they know its identifier?
quiz.explanation: The server must verify that the authenticated identity is allowed to perform the requested action on that object.

lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from Object-Level Authorization during authorized assessment and remediation work.

lessons.title: Role and Function-Level Authorization
lessons.description: Test admin routes, privileged actions and HTTP method changes without assuming the user interface is authoritative.
learningObjectives: Create role-based positive and negative tests.
Document authorization failures without causing destructive effects.
lessons.notes: A route may require authorization even if it is not linked in the client. Test server-side function checks explicitly.
lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from Role and Function-Level Authorization during authorized assessment and remediation work.

lessons.title: Business Logic and Workflow Abuse
lessons.description: Security bugs can arise when an application allows an action sequence that violates its intended business rules even though each individual request looks valid.
learningObjectives: Model sensitive workflows as state transitions.
lessons.notes: Business-logic assessment requires understanding the intended workflow. Examples include changing an account state without satisfying prerequisites or repeating a sensitive transition unexpectedly.
lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from Business Logic and Workflow Abuse during authorized assessment and remediation work.

tasks.title: Design a cross-user authorization regression suite
tasks.description: Create tests for two local test users accessing resources owned by each other.
tasks.problemStatement: A service must guarantee that authenticated users can view and modify only objects they are entitled to use.
objectives: Create same-user positive cases.
Create cross-user negative cases.
Cover both read and update operations.
Record expected HTTP status and body properties.
requirements: Use local test data only.
Test server-side behavior through the application interface.
Do not brute-force identifiers.
constraints: Keep the test data small and deterministic.
Do not treat obscurity of IDs as authorization.
tasks.hint: For every object test both owner and non-owner identities against the same resource.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The test design focuses on authorization outcomes. In the final project, the same principle is implemented by checking the authenticated user's ownership before read or update operations.

modules.assessment: The intern is assessed on server-side authorization reasoning and negative test coverage.

modules.title: Injection and Input Handling
modules.description: Understand SQL injection, command injection concepts, path traversal and safe input handling. Emphasize parameterized interfaces, allow-lists and contextual handling rather than blacklist-only defenses.
objectives: Recognize injection boundaries and dangerous sinks.
Use parameterized queries and safe APIs.
Explain why output encoding and input validation solve different problems.
Build regression tests for injection defenses.

lessons.title: Injection Boundaries and Safe APIs
lessons.description: Injection occurs when untrusted data changes the structure or meaning of an interpreted command. Learn common interpreter boundaries and safe API patterns.
learningObjectives: Use validation as a complementary control.
lessons.notes: OWASP places Injection at A05:2025 and recommends safe APIs, proper input validation and contextual handling. Blacklists alone are not a reliable primary defense.

quiz.question: What is the preferred defense against SQL injection when available?
quiz.explanation: Parameterized queries keep data separate from SQL syntax and are the primary defense described by OWASP.

lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from Injection Boundaries and Safe APIs during authorized assessment and remediation work.

lessons.title: SQL Injection Testing and Remediation
lessons.description: Learn how to recognize unsafe query construction, design safe test cases for a local lab, and remediate with parameter binding and least privilege.
learningObjectives: Compare unsafe and parameterized query patterns.
Write a regression test for a search or lookup endpoint.
lessons.notes: Never test arbitrary databases. Use the local training project and verify both the query implementation and observable behavior.
lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from SQL Injection Testing and Remediation during authorized assessment and remediation work.

lessons.title: XSS, Output Contexts and Template Safety
lessons.description: Study reflected and stored XSS, context-sensitive output encoding, safe templating and defense in depth such as CSP.
learningObjectives: Identify HTML, attribute, URL and script contexts.
Explain why CSP is defense in depth rather than the sole control.
lessons.notes: OWASP's XSS guidance emphasizes context-specific output encoding and warns against treating CSP as a complete XSS solution.

practicals.title: Validate an output-encoding boundary in a training application
instructions: Use a local intentionally vulnerable training page or a purpose-built test case only.
Trace one input from request parameter to rendered output.
Identify the rendering context as HTML text, attribute, URL or script data.
Demonstrate the difference between raw interpolation and context-appropriate encoding using inert test strings before using any executable payload in the lab.
Document the remediation and add a regression test.
practicals.deliverable: A data-flow diagram, remediation note and regression test reference.

quiz.question: Why is context important for output encoding?
options: All contexts use the same encoding
quiz.explanation: HTML text, attributes, URLs and script contexts have different parsing rules and therefore need appropriate handling.

lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from XSS, Output Contexts and Template Safety during authorized assessment and remediation work.

lessons.title: Path Traversal and Command Injection Concepts
lessons.description: Understand dangerous file-path and operating-system command construction and the role of allow-lists and safe APIs.
learningObjectives: Recognize tainted path and command inputs.
Explain why concatenating user input into commands is dangerous.
Prefer safe filesystem and process APIs.
lessons.notes: The internship focuses on controlled recognition and remediation, not weaponized exploitation. Test only purpose-built local cases.
lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from Path Traversal and Command Injection Concepts during authorized assessment and remediation work.

tasks.title: Refactor an unsafe SQLite lookup into a parameterized query
tasks.description: Replace string concatenation in a local Python SQLite lookup with a parameterized query and add regression tests.
tasks.problemStatement: A search function builds SQL from untrusted input using string concatenation. The goal is to separate data from SQL syntax and prove the behavior is preserved for normal input.
objectives: Use sqlite3 parameter binding.
Preserve expected search behavior.
Add tests for ordinary input and metacharacters.
Explain least-privilege considerations.
requirements: Use Python sqlite3.
Use an in-memory database for tests.
Do not expose or dump real data.
constraints: Do not rely on manual escaping as the primary fix.
Do not change business behavior unnecessarily.
tasks.hint: Replace string interpolation with placeholders and pass values separately.
tasks.solutionCode:
import sqlite3

def find_user(connection: sqlite3.Connection, username: str):
    cursor = connection.execute(
        "SELECT id, username, display_name FROM users WHERE username = ?",
        (username,)
    )
    return cursor.fetchone()

def test_find_user():
    connection = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    connection.execute("CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, username TEXT NOT NULL, display_name TEXT NOT NULL)")
    connection.execute("INSERT INTO users (username, display_name) VALUES (?, ?)", ("alice", "Alice"))
    connection.commit()
    assert find_user(connection, "alice")[1] == "alice"
    assert find_user(connection, "alice' OR '1'='1") is None
tasks.solutionExplanation: OWASP recommends prepared statements/parameterized queries as the preferred defense for SQL injection. Python sqlite3 accepts SQL and bound parameters separately.

modules.assessment: The intern must understand source-to-sink boundaries and safe API use.

modules.title: CSRF, SSRF, CORS, File Uploads and Security Headers
modules.description: Assess common browser/server interaction risks and configuration controls: CSRF, SSRF, CORS, upload validation and browser security headers.
objectives: Explain CSRF and appropriate defenses.
Recognize SSRF risk at URL-fetching boundaries.
Configure CORS deliberately rather than broadly.
Assess file upload and browser security headers using authoritative guidance.

lessons.title: CSRF and Request Authenticity
lessons.description: Learn how browser credentials can be sent with forged requests and how token, SameSite and Origin/Fetch Metadata controls can reduce risk.
learningObjectives: Explain synchronizer token and double-submit patterns.
Use defense in depth for sensitive requests.
lessons.notes: OWASP recommends token-based mitigations and discusses Fetch Metadata and SameSite as complementary controls. Do not treat a cookie flag as a complete CSRF design.
lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from CSRF and Request Authenticity during authorized assessment and remediation work.

lessons.title: SSRF and Safe URL Consumption
lessons.description: Understand the server-side request forgery boundary when a server fetches attacker-influenced URLs.
learningObjectives: Explain why network location validation is difficult.
Design allow-list and egress controls for controlled integrations.
lessons.notes: The safest design is often to avoid arbitrary server-side URL fetching. When business requirements need it, use strong allow-lists, DNS/IP handling, egress controls and logging.
lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from SSRF and Safe URL Consumption during authorized assessment and remediation work.

lessons.title: CORS and the Same-Origin Policy
lessons.description: Understand browser origin boundaries and deliberate cross-origin access.
learningObjectives: Explain what CORS does and does not protect.
Avoid reflecting arbitrary origins with credentials.
lessons.notes: CORS controls browser-enforced cross-origin access; it is not an authentication mechanism or a replacement for server-side authorization.

quiz.question: What is a major CORS anti-pattern?
options: Reflecting arbitrary Origin values while allowing credentials
quiz.answer: Reflecting arbitrary Origin values while allowing credentials
quiz.explanation: Credentialed cross-origin access must be deliberately scoped to trusted origins.

lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from CORS and the Same-Origin Policy during authorized assessment and remediation work.

lessons.title: File Upload Security
lessons.description: Learn allow-listed extensions, content-type and signature checks, safe file names, storage separation and size limits.
learningObjectives: Design a layered upload validation approach.
Store uploads safely and enforce resource limits.
lessons.notes: OWASP recommends multiple controls because file extensions and client-provided content types are weak signals by themselves.
lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from File Upload Security during authorized assessment and remediation work.

lessons.title: Security Headers and Transport
lessons.description: Assess CSP, HSTS, clickjacking controls, MIME sniffing protections and referrer policy.
learningObjectives: Distinguish current-response behavior from future browser policy where relevant.
Configure headers consistently with application behavior.
lessons.notes: HSTS tells browsers to use HTTPS for future requests to a host. MDN documents that HSTS affects future browser connections rather than the current response handling.

quiz.question: What does HSTS primarily instruct a browser to do?
options: Use HTTPS for future connections to the host
quiz.answer: Use HTTPS for future connections to the host
quiz.explanation: HSTS informs browsers that the host should only be accessed using HTTPS in future connections.

lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from Security Headers and Transport during authorized assessment and remediation work.

tasks.title: Build a security-header review table
tasks.description: Create a review function that classifies key response headers and records missing or inconsistent values for a local HTTPS deployment.
tasks.problemStatement: The security team needs a consistent way to review response headers without overstating what each header can protect against.
objectives: Check CSP, HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options and Referrer-Policy.
Record missing versus present headers.
Keep recommendations tied to the application's deployment model.
requirements: Use pure Python for the classifier.
Do not label HTTP responses as compliant with HSTS requirements.
Treat HSTS as relevant to HTTPS deployment.
constraints: Do not invent a universal CSP for every application.
Do not claim headers replace access control or validation.
tasks.hint: Start with an explicit list of security headers and evaluate them independently.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The review intentionally keeps HSTS tied to an HTTPS deployment context and treats headers as defense in depth rather than complete security boundaries.

modules.assessment: The intern must connect each control to the threat it actually addresses.

modules.title: Secure Code Review, Testing, Findings and Remediation
modules.description: Move from isolated vulnerability knowledge to engineering review: inspect code, write tests, triage findings, explain impact and verify fixes.
objectives: Conduct a structured secure code review.
Write unit and integration tests for security controls.
Produce evidence-based findings with remediation guidance.
Verify that fixes close the issue without introducing regressions.

lessons.title: Secure Code Review Method
lessons.description: Use an evidence-driven checklist covering validation, output handling, authentication, authorization, secrets, database access, file handling and error responses.
learningObjectives: Separate correctness bugs from security impact.
lessons.notes: OWASP's Secure Code Review Cheat Sheet provides practical review questions spanning input, output, file uploads, SQL injection, authentication and session management.
lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from Secure Code Review Method during authorized assessment and remediation work.

lessons.title: Security Testing with pytest
lessons.description: Create deterministic tests for security boundaries and run them in a local development environment.
learningObjectives: Write tests for expected and forbidden behavior.
Interpret failures without fabricating pass rates.
lessons.notes: Flask's testing guidance uses pytest and its test client for application tests. Tests should be deterministic and match actual application behavior.

quiz.question: What is a useful security regression test?
options: A test that asserts an unauthorized action is rejected
A test that only clicks visible buttons
A test that assumes the browser is secure
A test that ignores status codes
quiz.answer: A test that asserts an unauthorized action is rejected
quiz.explanation: Security regression tests should directly assert the application's control boundary.

lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from Security Testing with pytest during authorized assessment and remediation work.

lessons.title: Finding Triage and Severity Reasoning
lessons.description: Learn to describe evidence, affected asset, impact, exploitability assumptions, remediation and verification status without pretending to have measured more than you did.
lessons.notes: Use severity as a communication aid, not as a substitute for evidence. State assumptions and limitations.
lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from Finding Triage and Severity Reasoning during authorized assessment and remediation work.

lessons.title: Remediation Verification and Regression
lessons.description: A fix is not complete until the original case is retested and adjacent behavior is checked.
learningObjectives: Check for regressions around the fix.
lessons.notes: Security verification should compare the pre-fix expectation with the post-fix behavior and implementation controls.
lessons.summary: The intern should be able to apply the ideas from Remediation Verification and Regression during authorized assessment and remediation work.

tasks.title: Perform a focused secure code review
tasks.description: Review a small local Flask handler and identify input, authorization, session and error-handling concerns, then propose corrected code and tests.
tasks.problemStatement: A feature appears to work but has weak server-side controls. The review must identify the actual security boundary, recommend fixes and specify regression coverage.
objectives: Identify security-sensitive inputs and sinks.
Review authorization placement.
Check session and error-handling behavior.

project.heading: Build and Audit a Secure Case Management Web Application
project.description: Build a small authenticated case-management portal and then perform a structured web application security assessment against your own local instance. The application is designed to let an intern demonstrate request analysis, authentication and session review, server-side authorization, input validation, parameterized database access, CSRF protection, secure error handling, security headers, accessibility-aware UI construction, automated regression testing and evidence-based reporting. import os
from pathlib import Path
from flask import Flask, request

from .db import init_db
from .routes import register_routes

def create_app(test_config=None):
    app = Flask(__name__, instance_relative_config=True)
    app.config.from_mapping(
        SECRET_KEY=os.environ.get("SECRET_KEY", ""),
        DATABASE_PATH=os.environ.get("DATABASE_PATH", str(Path(app.instance_path) / "cases.db")),
        SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=os.environ.get("SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE", "false").lower() == "true",
        SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY=True,
        SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE="Lax",
        TRUSTED_HOSTS=[h.strip() for h in os.environ.get("TRUSTED_HOSTS", "localhost,127.0.0.1").split(",") if h.strip()],
    )

    if test_config:
        app.config.update(test_config)

    if not app.config["SECRET_KEY"]:
        if app.config.get("TESTING"):
            app.config["SECRET_KEY"] = "test-only-secret"
        elif os.environ.get("APP_ENV", "development") != "development":
            raise RuntimeError("SECRET_KEY must be configured outside development and tests")
        else:
            app.config["SECRET_KEY"] = "development-only-secret"

    Path(app.instance_path).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    init_db(app)

    @app.after_request
    def add_security_headers(response):
        response.headers.setdefault("X-Content-Type-Options", "nosniff")
        response.headers.setdefault("Content-Security-Policy", "default-src 'self'; style-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'")
        response.headers.setdefault("Referrer-Policy", "no-referrer")
        response.headers.setdefault("X-Frame-Options", "DENY")
        if request.is_secure:
            response.headers.setdefault("Strict-Transport-Security", "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains")
        return response

    register_routes(app)
    return app

fileWiseSolution.code:
import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path
from flask import current_app, g

SCHEMA = """
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    username TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    password_hash TEXT NOT NULL,
    role TEXT NOT NULL CHECK(role IN ('user', 'admin'))
);
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cases (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    owner_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
    title TEXT NOT NULL,
    details TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    FOREIGN KEY(owner_id) REFERENCES users(id)
);
"""

def get_db():
    if "db" not in g:
        database = Path(current_app.config["DATABASE_PATH"])
        database.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        g.db = sqlite3.connect(database)
        g.db.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
        g.db.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")
    return g.db

def close_db(_exception=None):
    db = g.pop("db", None)
    if db is not None:
        db.close()

def init_db(app):
    with app.app_context():
        db = get_db()
        db.executescript(SCHEMA)
        from werkzeug.security import generate_password_hash
        users = [
            ("alice", generate_password_hash("training-alice-password"), "user"),
            ("bob", generate_password_hash("training-bob-password"), "user"),
            ("admin", generate_password_hash("training-admin-password"), "admin"),
        ]
        for username, password_hash, role in users:
            db.execute(
                "INSERT OR IGNORE INTO users (username, password_hash, role) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
                (username, password_hash, role),
            )
        db.commit()
    app.teardown_appcontext(close_db)

from tests.conftest import csrf, login

def test_login_success(client):
    response = login(client, "alice", "training-alice-password")
    assert response.status_code == 200
    assert b"Your cases" in response.data

def test_login_failure_is_generic(client):
    response = login(client, "alice", "wrong-password")
    assert response.status_code == 401
    assert b"Invalid username or password" in response.data
    assert b"Traceback" not in response.data

def test_csrf_required_for_case_creation(client):
    login(client, "alice", "training-alice-password")
    response = client.post("/cases", data={"title": "Test", "details": "Details"})
    assert response.status_code == 400

def test_owner_can_create_and_read_case(client):
    login(client, "alice", "training-alice-password")
    token = csrf(client)
    created = client.post("/cases", data={"title": "Private case", "details": "Alice detail", "csrf_token": token}, follow_redirects=True)
    assert created.status_code == 200
    with client.session_transaction() as session:
        assert session["user_id"] == 1
    response = client.get("/dashboard")
    assert b"Private case" in response.data

def test_other_user_cannot_read_owner_case(client, app):
    login(client, "alice", "training-alice-password")
    token = csrf(client)
    client.post("/cases", data={"title": "Alice private", "details": "Secret detail", "csrf_token": token})
    with app.app_context():
        from app.db import get_db
        case_id = get_db().execute("SELECT id FROM cases WHERE owner_id = 1 ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1").fetchone()["id"]
    client.post("/logout", data={"csrf_token": csrf(client)})
    login(client, "bob", "training-bob-password")
    response = client.get(f"/cases/{case_id}")
    assert response.status_code == 403
    assert b"Secret detail" not in response.data

def test_non_admin_cannot_access_admin_route(client):
    login(client, "alice", "training-alice-password")
    response = client.get("/admin/cases")
    assert response.status_code == 403

def test_admin_can_access_admin_route(client):
    login(client, "admin", "training-admin-password")
    response = client.get("/admin/cases")
    assert response.status_code == 200
    assert b"All cases" in response.data

def test_security_headers(client):
    response = client.get("/")
    assert response.headers["X-Content-Type-Options"] == "nosniff"
    assert response.headers["Content-Security-Policy"]
    assert response.headers["Referrer-Policy"] == "no-referrer"

def test_cookie_configuration(app):
    assert app.config["SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY"] is True
    assert app.config["SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE"] == "Lax"

fileWiseSolution.code:
# Secure Case Portal

A small local training application for the Web Application Security Internship. The project is intentionally scoped to loopback addresses and uses SQLite for local data.

## Safety boundary

Run and assess this application only on your own machine or another environment where you have explicit permission. Do not point the included test workflow at public sites.

## Setup

1. Create and activate a Python 3.11+ virtual environment.
2. Install the project: `python -m pip install -e .`
3. Copy `.env.example` to `.env` and set a development-only secret.
4. Start the app with `python app.py`.
5. Browse to `http://127.0.0.1:5000/`.

## Test accounts

The local seed creates three training identities: `alice`, `bob`, and `admin`. Their training passwords are defined in `app/db.py` and are not intended for any external deployment.

## Tests

Run `pytest`. The suite covers CSRF enforcement, ownership authorization, admin authorization, login failure handling and security headers.

## Security review workflow

Review the application with browser developer tools or an intercepting proxy. Inventory endpoints, compare authenticated and unauthenticated behavior, test owner versus non-owner access using the local training identities, inspect cookie attributes, review security headers and verify that state-changing routes reject missing CSRF tokens.

## Deployment boundary

The Flask development server is for local training. For production, use a supported production WSGI server and HTTPS termination appropriate to the deployment environment. Reconfigure the session cookie Secure flag and secret management for production.
